Isaiah 34.audience: An oracle against all nations and especially Edom, Judah's neighbor to the southeast, whose land is made desolate.

culture.title: Bozrah
culture.text: Bozrah was a chief city of Edom, in the hills south of the Dead Sea.

culture.title: Burning pitch and brimstone
culture.text: Edom's land becomes burning pitch and sulphur, like the region of Sodom near the Dead Sea, where bitumen and sulphur are found.

culture.title: Desert creatures
culture.text: Pelicans (cormorants), bitterns, owls, ravens, dragons (jackals), and wild beasts take over the ruins.

Isaiah 35.audience: Isaiah promises that the desert will bloom and the redeemed will return to Zion on a highway called "The way of holiness" (Isaiah 35:8).

culture.title: The glory of Lebanon, Carmel, and Sharon
culture.text: Lebanon's forests, Carmel's ridge, and the plain of Sharon were the greenest regions of the land.

culture.title: Waters in the wilderness
culture.text: Springs in dry land and parched ground turned to pools describe the reversal of desert conditions.

Isaiah 36.audience: Isaiah 36–39 tells of Hezekiah's reign in narrative and repeats, almost word for word, 2 Kings 18:13–20:19. Sennacherib invaded Judah in 701 BC.

culture.title: The Rabshakeh
culture.text: Rabshakeh is an Assyrian title, ‘chief cupbearer,’ a high officer who spoke for the king.

culture.title: Egypt as a broken reed
culture.text: "The staff of this broken reed, on Egypt"—a cracked reed cane that pierces the hand of anyone leaning on it.

culture.title: Speaking in Aramaic
culture.text: Judah's officials ask Rabshakeh to speak Aramaic ("the Syrian language"), the diplomatic language, not Hebrew, which the people on the wall understood.

Isaiah 37.audience: Hezekiah prays over Sennacherib's letter, and Isaiah promises that the king of Assyria will not enter Jerusalem. The account repeats 2 Kings 19.

culture.title: Sennacherib's annals
culture.text: Sennacherib's own records list forty-six cities of Judah captured and boast of shutting Hezekiah up ‘like a bird in a cage,’ but do not claim the capture of Jerusalem.

culture.title: Gods made of wood and stone
culture.text: Assyria burned the gods of conquered nations "for they were no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone."

Isaiah 38.audience: Hezekiah is sick to the point of death and is given fifteen more years. His written prayer of thanksgiving is preserved here (Isaiah 38:9–20).

culture.title: Turning to the wall
culture.text: Hezekiah turns his face to the wall to pray privately.

culture.title: A shepherd's tent and a weaver's loom
culture.text: Life taken down like a shepherd's tent, and cut off like a weaver cutting finished cloth from the loom.

culture.title: The dial of Ahaz
culture.text: The shadow goes back ten degrees on the steps ("dial") of Ahaz, used to tell the time by the sun.

Isaiah 39.audience: Envoys from Merodachbaladan of Babylon visit Hezekiah, and Isaiah foretells that Babylon will carry off Judah's treasures and descendants (Isaiah 39:6–7).

culture.title: Merodachbaladan
culture.text: Merodachbaladan (Marduk-apla-iddina II) was a Chaldean ruler who seized Babylon and rebelled against Assyria for years, seeking allies in the west.

culture.title: Showing the treasure house
culture.text: Hezekiah shows the envoys his silver, gold, spices, oil, and armory—signs of a valuable ally.

Isaiah 40.audience: Isaiah 40 begins with "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people" (Isaiah 40:1) and speaks of Jerusalem's warfare accomplished. All four Gospels apply verse 3 to John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4; John 1:23).

culture.title: Preparing a highway
culture.text: Before a king's visit, roads were leveled and straightened. Babylonian kings built processional ways for their gods.

culture.title: A shepherd carrying lambs
culture.text: Shepherds carried newborn lambs in the fold of their cloaks and led ewes with young gently.

culture.title: Making an idol
culture.text: Craftsmen cast idols in metal, overlaid them with gold, or carved them from wood that would not rot, then fixed them so they would not fall over.

Isaiah 41.audience: God addresses Israel as "my servant" and "the seed of Abraham my friend" (Isaiah 41:8) and speaks of a conqueror raised up from the east.

culture.title: A threshing sledge
culture.text: A threshing sledge was a heavy board studded with stones or iron teeth, dragged over grain to break the stalks.

culture.title: Craftsmen encouraging each other
culture.text: The carpenter, goldsmith, and metalworker cheer each other on and nail the idol so it won't move.

Isaiah 42.audience: The first of the Servant Songs (Isaiah 42:1–9). Matthew quotes verses 1–4 of Jesus (Matthew 12:17–21).

culture.title: A bruised reed and smoking flax
culture.text: A reed was a cheap pen or measuring rod; a flax wick smoldered in an oil lamp. A damaged reed was usually snapped and a smoking wick snuffed out.

culture.title: Prisoners in darkness
culture.text: Ancient prisons were often dark pits or dungeons.

Isaiah 43.audience: God tells Israel, "Fear not: for I have redeemed thee" (Isaiah 43:1), and promises to bring their children from east, west, north, and south.

culture.title: A ransom of nations
culture.text: "I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee." Egypt, Ethiopia (Cush), and Seba were the great lands to the south.

culture.title: Ships of the Chaldeans
culture.text: Babylon's trade moved by boat on the Euphrates and its canals.

culture.title: Sweet cane and fat of sacrifices
culture.text: Sweet cane (calamus) was an imported spice used in the anointing oil (Exodus 30:23).

Isaiah 44.audience: Isaiah mocks idol-making and names Cyrus as the one who will say of Jerusalem, "Thou shalt be built" (Isaiah 44:28). Cyrus' decree is recorded in Ezra 1.

culture.title: Half for fire, half for a god
culture.text: A man burns half a log to bake bread and warm himself and carves the rest into a god to worship.

culture.title: Writing on the hand
culture.text: "Another shall subscribe with his hand unto the LORD"—slaves were sometimes marked on the hand with their owner's name.

Isaiah 45.audience: God calls Cyrus "his anointed" (Isaiah 45:1), a Persian king who would free the exiles. Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

culture.title: Gates of bronze
culture.text: Babylon's gates were massive and bronze-plated. Herodotus describes a hundred bronze gates in Babylon's walls.

culture.title: Treasures of darkness
culture.text: Conquered kings' hidden treasuries became the property of the conqueror. Cyrus took the wealth of Croesus of Lydia and of Babylon.

culture.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
culture.text: Cyrus' own inscription says he returned exiled peoples and their gods to their homes—the same policy Isaiah describes.

Isaiah 46.audience: Isaiah describes Babylon's gods Bel and Nebo being carried away on animals as Babylon falls (Isaiah 46:1).

culture.title: Bel and Nebo
culture.text: Bel (Marduk) was Babylon's chief god and Nebo (Nabu) his son, god of writing. Their images were carried in procession at the Babylonian new year festival.

culture.title: Gods carried as burdens
culture.text: Idols had to be carried and set in place; they could not move or save. Israel's God carries his people instead (Isaiah 46:3–4).

Isaiah 47.audience: A taunt song against Babylon, "the lady of kingdoms" (Isaiah 47:5), who will sit in the dust.

culture.title: Grinding meal
culture.text: "Take the millstones, and grind meal"—the work of a slave girl. The proud queen becomes a servant.

culture.title: Astrologers and stargazers
culture.text: Babylon was famous for astrology and omen-reading. Babylonian scribes kept records of the stars and monthly predictions.

Isaiah 48.audience: God tells Israel to "go ye forth of Babylon, flee ye from the Chaldeans" (Isaiah 48:20).

culture.title: Refined in the furnace of affliction
culture.text: Silver was refined in a furnace. God has "chosen thee in the furnace of affliction."

culture.title: Water from the rock
culture.text: The return is compared to the exodus, when water came from the rock (Exodus 17:6).

Isaiah 49.audience: The second Servant Song (Isaiah 49:1–13). Paul applies verse 6, "a light to the Gentiles," to his own mission (Acts 13:47).

culture.title: A polished arrow
culture.text: An archer kept his best arrow polished and hidden in his quiver until needed.

culture.title: Engraved on the palms
culture.text: "I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands"—marks on the hand served as reminders.

culture.title: Kings as nursing fathers
culture.text: Kings and queens will care for Israel's children; bowing down and licking the dust was the language of total submission (Psalm 72:9).

Isaiah 50.audience: The third Servant Song (Isaiah 50:4–11). The servant gives his back to smiters and his cheeks to those who pluck the hair.

culture.title: A bill of divorcement
culture.text: A husband who divorced his wife gave her a written certificate (Deuteronomy 24:1). God asks where Zion's certificate is.

culture.title: Plucking the beard
culture.text: Pulling out a man's beard was an insult and an assault (Nehemiah 13:25).

Isaiah 51.audience: God calls his people to look to Abraham and Sarah, "the rock whence ye are hewn" (Isaiah 51:1), and to awake.

culture.title: Cutting Rahab
culture.text: Rahab and the dragon are images of the sea and of Egypt, defeated at the exodus (Isaiah 51:10).

culture.title: The cup of trembling
culture.text: Jerusalem has drunk "the cup of his fury"—the cup of God's wrath, now taken away and given to her enemies.

culture.title: Walking on the backs
culture.text: Conquerors made captives lie down so they could walk over them—a scene shown in ancient art.

Isaiah 52.audience: Isaiah announces good tidings to Zion. Paul quotes verse 7 of gospel preachers (Romans 10:15). The fourth Servant Song begins at Isaiah 52:13.

culture.title: Beautiful feet on the mountains
culture.text: Runners carried news of battles across the hills. Watchmen on the walls saw them coming.

culture.title: Shaking off the dust
culture.text: Captives sat in the dust with bands on their necks; Zion is told to rise and loose them.

Isaiah 53.audience: The fourth Servant Song continues (Isaiah 52:13–53:12). The New Testament quotes it often (Matthew 8:17; Luke 22:37; John 12:38; Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:22–25).

culture.title: A root out of dry ground
culture.text: A shoot growing from dry, hard ground looks weak and unpromising.

culture.title: A lamb to the slaughter
culture.text: Sheep are silent when shorn or led to slaughter. Lambs were offered daily at the temple.

culture.title: With the rich in his death
culture.text: Criminals were usually buried in common graves. Jesus was buried in the tomb of a rich man, Joseph of Arimathaea (Matthew 27:57–60).

Isaiah 54.audience: Zion is pictured as a barren woman who will have many children. Paul quotes verse 1 in Galatians 4:27.

culture.title: Enlarging the tent
culture.text: Herders made their tents larger by adding curtains, lengthening cords, and driving stakes deeper.

culture.title: Stones laid with fair colours
culture.text: The city is rebuilt with sapphires, agates, and carbuncles—images used again for the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:18–21).

Isaiah 55.audience: God invites everyone who thirsts to come, buy, and eat without money, and offers "the sure mercies of David" (Isaiah 55:3; Acts 13:34).

culture.title: Water sellers
culture.text: In cities, water, wine, and milk were sold in the markets.

culture.title: Rain and snow returning
culture.text: Rain and snow water the ground and give seed and bread; God's word does not return empty.

culture.title: Fir instead of thorn
culture.text: Fir and myrtle replacing thorns and briers reverse the curse of the ground (Genesis 3:18).

Isaiah 56.audience: God welcomes foreigners and eunuchs who keep his sabbaths. Jesus quotes verse 7, "mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people," when cleansing the temple (Mark 11:17).

culture.title: Eunuchs
culture.text: Eunuchs served in royal courts but were excluded from the congregation (Deuteronomy 23:1). Isaiah promises them a place and a name.

culture.title: Dumb watchdogs
culture.text: Israel's leaders are like watchdogs that cannot bark—guard dogs that fail to warn.

Isaiah 57.audience: Isaiah condemns idolatry practiced under green trees and in valleys, and promises peace to the humble and contrite.

culture.title: Smooth stones of the stream
culture.text: Offerings were poured out on smooth stones in stream beds as part of pagan worship.

culture.title: Sacrificing children in the valleys
culture.text: Children were sacrificed "in the valleys under the clifts of the rocks," as in the valley of Hinnom (Jeremiah 7:31).

Isaiah 58.audience: God contrasts empty fasting with true fasting: freeing the oppressed, feeding the hungry, and sheltering the poor.

culture.title: Fasting days
culture.text: People fasted with sackcloth and ashes and bowed their heads like a bulrush. After the exile, fasts were kept to mourn the fall of Jerusalem (Zechariah 7:3–5).

culture.title: Breaking every yoke
culture.text: The yoke was a wooden beam on the neck of oxen, a picture of oppression and forced labor.

Isaiah 59.audience: Isaiah describes how sin has separated the people from God and pictures the LORD putting on armor to bring justice. Paul quotes verses 7–8 in Romans 3:15–17.

culture.title: Cockatrice eggs and spider webs
culture.text: Their schemes are like hatching viper eggs and weaving spider webs—deadly and useless.

culture.title: God's armor
culture.text: The breastplate of righteousness and helmet of salvation reappear in Paul's description of the armor of God (Ephesians 6:14–17).

Isaiah 60.audience: Zion is told to "arise, shine; for thy light is come" (Isaiah 60:1), and nations bring their wealth to her.

culture.title: Camels of Midian and gifts of Sheba
culture.text: Caravans of camels from Midian, Ephah, and Sheba bring gold and incense—the trade goods of Arabia.

culture.title: Doves to their windows
culture.text: Ships sail toward Zion like doves flying home to their dovecotes.

culture.title: Gates open continually
culture.text: City gates were shut at night. Gates never shut picture lasting peace (Revelation 21:25).

Isaiah 61.audience: The speaker says the Spirit of the Lord is upon him to proclaim liberty. Jesus read verses 1–2 in the synagogue at Nazareth and said, "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears" (Luke 4:21).

culture.title: The acceptable year
culture.text: "The acceptable year of the LORD" recalls the jubilee, when liberty was proclaimed and land returned (Leviticus 25:10).

culture.title: Beauty for ashes
culture.text: Mourners put ashes on their heads; a garland ("beauty") and oil of joy replace them.

culture.title: Bridegroom and bride adorned
culture.text: Bridegrooms wore a turban or garland and brides jewels on their wedding day.

Isaiah 62.audience: Zion receives new names, Hephzibah (‘my delight is in her’) and Beulah (‘married’) (Isaiah 62:4).

culture.title: A crown in God's hand
culture.text: Zion becomes "a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, and a royal diadem."

culture.title: Watchmen on the walls
culture.text: Watchmen stood on city walls day and night; here they keep reminding God of his promise.

Isaiah 63.audience: A figure comes from Edom with garments stained red, and the prophet recalls the exodus and prays for God's help.

culture.title: Treading the winepress
culture.text: Grapes were trodden underfoot in rock-cut winepresses, staining clothes red. Revelation uses the image (Revelation 19:13–15).

culture.title: Bozrah and Edom
culture.text: Bozrah was a city of Edom. Edom's name sounds like the Hebrew for ‘red.’

Isaiah 64.audience: A prayer of confession: "we are the clay, and thou our potter" (Isaiah 64:8). Paul echoes verse 4 in 1 Corinthians 2:9.

culture.title: Filthy rags
culture.text: "Our righteousnesses are as filthy rags"—garments stained and unclean.

culture.title: The burned temple
culture.text: "Our holy and our beautiful house... is burned up with fire"—the temple in ruins.

Isaiah 65.audience: God answers with judgment on idolaters and a promise of "new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17), taken up in Revelation 21:1.

culture.title: Sacrificing in gardens and among graves
culture.text: Some burned incense in gardens, sat among graves to consult the dead, and ate pig's flesh—practices of pagan worship.

culture.title: Gad and Meni
culture.text: The "troop" and "number" are the gods Gad (Fortune) and Meni (Destiny), for whom tables of food and drink were set.

culture.title: Building and planting
culture.text: In war, invaders often occupied houses and ate the fruit of vineyards others had planted (Deuteronomy 28:30). Here the builder lives in his own house.

Isaiah 66.audience: The book ends with God gathering all nations to see his glory. Jesus quotes verse 24, "their worm dieth not," in Mark 9:48.

culture.title: Heaven my throne, earth my footstool
culture.text: Stephen quotes this verse in his speech about the temple (Acts 7:49–50).

culture.title: Mourning to a mother's comfort
culture.text: Jerusalem is pictured as a mother nursing her children and carrying them on her hip.

culture.title: Tarshish, Pul, and Lud
culture.text: Tarshish, Pul, Lud, Tubal, and Javan (Greece) represent distant peoples to the west and north.
